query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A precise, short-duration annealing treatment applied immediately after casting can refine the interlamellar spacing and enhance the coherence of the phase interfaces in eutectic HEAs, thereby simultaneously increasing strength and ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, e.g., with a yield strength of approximately 944 MPa and ductility around 25%.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled, short-duration thermal annealing treatment at an optimized temperature immediately after solidification.
generation.conditions: Ambient (room temperature) mechanical testing under typical engineering strain rates, suitable for structural applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Interlamellar spacing and the coherence of the interfaces between the alternating fcc and B2 lamellae.
generation.mechanism: The brief annealing induces limited atomic diffusion that refines the lamellar spacing and reinforces the bonding at phase interfaces. This structural refinement increases dislocation blocking (boosting strength) while allowing more uniform plastic flow (improving ductility), thereby mitigating the traditional strength–ductility trade-off.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-cast state, the treated alloy is expected to demonstrate moderate improvements (on the order of 10–20%) in both yield strength and ductility.
generation.baseline: The as-cast eutectic HEA, exhibiting an fcc/B2 dual-phase lamellar microstructure with typical mechanical properties (e.g., ~944 MPa yield strength and ~25% ductility).
generation.boundary: This effect is anticipated to hold for eutectic high-entropy alloys with similar dual-phase lamellar microstructures under ambient test conditions. Its applicability to other alloy systems or extreme temperature regimes is not yet established.
generation.uncertainty: Exact annealing temperature, duration, and quantitative improvement levels require further optimization and may vary with specific alloy compositions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same batch of eutectic HEA: one set undergoes the short-duration annealing treatment immediately post-casting, while the control set remains as-cast. Subject both sets to identical room temperature tensile testing and microstructural characterization.
measurements: Interlamellar spacing and phase interface coherence via SEM/TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show statistically significant improvements (approximately 10–20%) in both yield strength and ductility, or if microstructural analysis does not confirm a refined interlamellar spacing with enhanced interface coherence compared to the as-cast samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

decision.trend: The earliest work on eutectic HEAs (PMC4145285) demonstrated that an as‐cast lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure could deliver a notable balance between strength (~944 MPa) and ductility (≈25%) at room temperature. Subsequent processing—such as moderate cold rolling—has been used to boost strength further (to around 1265 MPa) but at the cost of lowering ductility. In parallel, other studies in HEAs (often using multi‐step alloying or complex thermo‐mechanical treatments) have attempted to overcome the classic strength–ductility trade-off, but they tend to separate the interventions for strengthening and ductility improvement rather than unifying them in a single process.
decision.unsolved: No singular intervention has yet been identified for eutectic HEAs that simultaneously optimizes the dual-phase (lamellar) microstructure to enhance both dislocation blocking (strength) and interface compliance (ductility) without resorting to multistep processing or separate alloying modifications.
decision.lever: Implement a precise, short-duration annealing treatment immediately post-solidification to tune the interlamellar spacing and enhance the coherence of phase interfaces
decision.why: This approach builds directly on the observed benefits of the eutectic lamellar structure by targeting its fine features in a single thermal step. Controlled annealing can refine the spacing and adjust interface characteristics to simultaneously impede dislocation motion (boosting strength) while allowing more uniform plastic flow (preserving or improving ductility), thereby addressing the unresolved strength–ductility trade-off in a singular, process-level intervention.
